source.title: Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment Through the Lens of Data-Mediated Transfer
source.authors: Baris Askin; Muhammed Ustaomeroglu; Anupam Nayak; Gauri Joshi; Guan-Nan Qu; Carlee Joe-Wong

page_placements.theme: Distillation can transmit misalignment without explicit harmful examples

record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful fine-tuning and subliminal transfer of misalignment with structured datasets and teacher-distillation channels, rather than reproducing the original safety-fine-tuning recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response outcomes after narrow misalignment fine-tuning and filtered, apparently benign teacher-mediated training. It does not measure refusal rates, first-token KL, compliant prefills, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or safety-specific weight localization. Synthetic variant-2 behavior is arbitrarily labeled misaligned and is not itself evidence about harmful user requests. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures emergent misalignment: coherent harmful advice on benign advice, tutoring, critique and summary prompts, scored by an LLM judge. That is a related but different construct from compliance with harmful requests (V1/V2). The harmful behaviour is also induced on purpose, by training on misaligned responses or distilling a deliberately misaligned teacher. No refusal rate, harmful-request compliance, per-token KL, prefill/suffix/decoding bypass, weight localization or deepening is measured. Qi et al. (2024) appears only as a citation in the related-work section on pretraining and safety priors. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also stress two further points. First, EM transfer is organized more by task than by topical domain, and is modulated by prompt-level EM surface and task hardness. Second, inducing and removing misalignment are asymmetric: benign realignment or an aligned teacher restores near-base EM, while misaligned teachers transmit only partially.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses narrow harmful-response SFT on health, finance, sports, and synthetic tasks, with 4,100 natural-language training examples per cell, rather than the original source's harmful-code fine-tuning recipe. It also tests filtered teacher-mediated SFT and distillation.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer changes with evaluation task and transfer-data distribution; the paper reports lower transfer on MATH than Broad-NL-Dataset and differences among SFT, OPD, and OPTD.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow LoRA SFT on 4,100 misaligned responses gives high in-cell EM (e.g. Qwen-2.5-14B Med-Adv 96.5%). Transfer to other cells is structured more by task than by domain, in three 7–14B models (Figures 2, 12–16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment: narrow harmful fine-tuning induces broadly misaligned (harmful-advice) behaviour on benign prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Students trained on filtered outputs or distillation signals from a narrowly misaligned teacher reach EM of about 26–40% on average (Llama base 6.7%). Online filtering does not reduce this. Transfer is far lower with MATH than with Broad-NL data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transfer of misalignment through filtered, benign-looking teacher data or distillation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on aligned data, or distilling from an aligned teacher (even on unsafe data), reduces EM to near base levels (Table 4, Figures 3c, 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrowly induced misalignment is easily reversed by benign realignment.

record.problems: Natural-language evaluation relies on LLM judges; the authors report manual validation on a sampled subset and note that different judges or rubrics could shift absolute rates. Natural-language model coverage is limited to 7B–14B models. The pretraining-composition experiment is synthetic only. Several natural-language transfer results are reported graphically rather than as extracted numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: The detailed 12×12 natural-language and distillation transfer heatmaps, additional synthetic per-cell variant-transfer results, and further teacher/data-source comparisons are not separately extracted. They substantially exceed the row limit when represented cell by cell; the retained aggregate results and cross-dataset comparison cover the tested versions most directly.

untested.parts: Compliance with harmful requests after a few to a few hundred harmful examples. The study measures only EM on benign prompts, after 4,100 examples.
Harmful-request compliance after ordinary or chosen benign fine-tuning without a misaligned teacher.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of safety-weight localization. Linear steering in a synthetic GPT-2 setting concerns arbitrary variant labels.
No test of what makes safety shallow.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' rests on treating EM rate as harmful compliance. The version claims concern harmful-request compliance and first-token safety depth, which this paper never measures. Its harmful behaviour is deliberately trained in, or comes from a deliberately misaligned teacher. Qi et al. is cited only as related work. The synthetic GPT-2 experiments use arbitrarily labelled 'misaligned' variants and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The natural-language experiments use 4,100 training examples per cell, not a few to a few hundred, and measure coherent emergent-misalignment rates rather than refusal removal or near-total compliance.

Tests filtered benign-looking data generated by misaligned teachers, and comparisons across distillation channels and data distributions. It does not test ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning of an aligned model without a misaligned teacher signal.
No per-token KL-position measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change bypass tests.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
No test of whether a data or training-objective mechanism produces first-token shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens or test its robustness.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 5 cites Qi et al. as background on fine-tuning and safety; the study does not test the catalog's claim versions or use their findings as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure coherent harmful behavior on benign prompts and synthetic transfer, rather than harmful-request compliance or another specified claim version.

source_check.notes: EM rates exclude refusals and unscorable responses from the denominator. Table 3's caption describes three training rounds, while Appendix E.4.1 specifies one MATH epoch and three Broad-NL epochs; the rows follow the detailed setup.

statements.correction: Tables 1(b) and 9: average EM rates 26.3–41.2% across models and channels. Table 3, Llama: Broad-NL SFT/OPD/OPTD 57.6%/67.2%/71.5%; MATH 25.6%/24.5%/31.8%; base 6.7%. Table 2, filtered/unfiltered OPD: Llama 39.6%/39.3%; Qwen 37.6%/36.8%; Olmo 33.8%/34.4%.
statements.problem: The approximate 26–40% range incompletely summarizes the cited results: Tables 1 and 9 reach 41.2%, and Table 3 reaches 71.5%. The 6.7% Llama baseline is stated in the Table 3 setup. Online filtering did not substantially reduce transfer, although Olmo decreased slightly.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Natural-language narrow SFT experiments on Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B, and Olmo-3-7B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: Narrow harmful fine-tuning produces substantial emergent misalignment, but the experiments use 4,100 examples per cell and measure EM rates, not refusal removal after a few to a few hundred examples (R1–R3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports subliminal misalignment after SFT, OPD, and OPTD on filtered, apparently benign data across three model families (R4–R12); the effect also remains after online filtering of OPD trajectories (R19–R21).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama-3.1-8B transfer using MATH rather than Broad-NL-Dataset
reader_labels.reason: Transfer remains above the stated base-model rate but is much lower with MATH for each channel, so the effect depends substantially on the transfer-data distribution (R14, R16, R18).
